lead: A practical source has internal resistance, so its terminal voltage sags as the load draws more current. Two circuits reproduce that sag exactly: a voltage source in series with a resistor, or a current source in parallel with the same resistor. Swapping one for the other, using I_s = V_s/R_s, is source transformation. It exists to make circuits easier to reduce before mesh or nodal analysis. It is used whenever a circuit mixes current sources and voltage sources, and it is the step behind Norton and Thevenin equivalents.
prereq: You need: source symbols and reference directions from 1.2, and series-parallel reduction with the current divider from 1.5.

sections.h3: Two models, one pair of terminals

blocks.text: A real source is not ideal. A cell, a lead-acid battery, a bench supply, each has some internal resistance. Charge pushed through that resistance loses part of the EMF as heat, so the terminal voltage falls as the load draws more current. Two circuits reproduce this fall, and from outside they are indistinguishable.

Model A is an ideal voltage source V_s in series with a resistance R_s. Write KVL round the loop: V = V_s − I·R_s. V is the terminal voltage in volts, V_s is the source EMF in volts, I is the current delivered to the load in amperes, and R_s is the internal resistance in ohms.
Model B is an ideal current source I_s in parallel with the same R_s. KCL at the top node gives I = I_s − V/R_s. Multiply by R_s and rearrange: V = I_s·R_s − I·R_s.

Compare the two lines. They are the same line when V_s = I_s·R_s. So the pair (V_s with R_s in series) and the pair (I_s with R_s in parallel) share one terminal V-I curve, one open-circuit voltage, one short-circuit current. Only the inside differs, and the load never sees the inside.

sections.h3: The rule, the arrow, the steps

blocks.text: I_s = V_s / R_s        V_s = I_s · R_s
blocks.where: I_s is the transformed current source in amperes; V_s is the original voltage source in volts; R_s is the same resistance in ohms, moved from series to parallel or the reverse. Some syllabi call this source conversion.

items: Find the practical source: an ideal source with a resistance in series (voltage form) or in parallel (current form).
Read off R_s. Its value does not change; only its position changes.
Compute the new source value with I_s = V_s/R_s, or V_s = I_s·R_s.
Redraw: the series resistor becomes a parallel resistor, the parallel resistor becomes a series resistor.
Point the current arrow at the node that was the + terminal of the voltage source. Reversing that gives the same magnitude with the wrong sign everywhere later.
Continue with series-parallel reduction from 1.5, or with mesh and nodal analysis from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Direction loses the most marks. Inside a current source the arrow points from the negative terminal to the positive terminal, so the current leaves the + terminal into the external circuit, exactly as the + terminal of a voltage source delivers current outwards. The node that was + stays +.

Two cases refuse the swap. An ideal voltage source has R_s = 0, so I_s = V_s/0 is infinite and no finite current source matches it. An ideal current source has nothing in parallel, R_s = infinity, so V_s = infinity. Only practical sources with a finite, non-zero resistance transform.
Its job is to make everything look alike before you solve. Nodal analysis likes current sources feeding nodes; mesh analysis likes voltage sources round loops. Convert, merge, then write equations.

items: Voltage sources in series add. Current sources in parallel add, provided their arrows point the same way; opposite arrows subtract.
A branch with a voltage source and a series resistor becomes a current source whose parallel resistor joins the neighbouring parallel group directly.
The Norton current of a one-port is the short-circuit current, which is the I_s you get by transforming the Thevenin form. Dependent-source versions are handled in Unit 2.
The load stays outside the transformation. The equivalence is only what the two kept terminals see; a resistor you transform cannot also be the load.
Terminal V and I are preserved, internal power is not. In the worked example the voltage model's source delivers 64 W and the current model's delivers 32 W, while the load takes 21.33 W in both.

figure.caption: The 24 V source with its 6 Ω series resistor and the 4 A source with its 6 Ω parallel resistor are the same two terminals; the 3 Ω load draws 2.667 A at 8 V from either one.

spec.title: Source transformation
spec.aria: A 24 V source with a 6 ohm series resistor is replaced by a 4 A source with a 6 ohm parallel resistor, and both drive the same 3 ohm load at 2.667 A and 8 V.

examples.question: A 24 V source has 6 Ω in series with it and feeds a 3 Ω load. (a) Find the load current and load voltage directly. (b) Transform the source and find the same two quantities from the current-source model. (c) Confirm the two models agree.
steps: The 6 Ω series resistor and the 3 Ω load are in series. Total resistance = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω.
Load current I = V_s / (R_s + R_load) = 24/9 = 2.6667 A.
Load voltage V_load = I × R_load = 2.6667 × 3 = 8 V.
Transform: I_s = V_s / R_s = 24/6 = 4 A, placed in parallel with the same 6 Ω.
Now the 6 Ω and the 3 Ω are in parallel across the current source. The current divider gives load current = 4 × 6/(6 + 3) = 4 × 0.6667 = 2.6667 A.
The arrow points at the node that was the + terminal of the 24 V source, that is, towards the load.
Both models give 2.6667 A and 8 V, so the terminal behaviour is unchanged.
examples.answer: Load current is 2.6667 A and load voltage is 8 V from both models; the equivalent current source is I_s = 4 A in parallel with 6 Ω.
examples.check:
Vs = 24.0
Rs = 6.0
Rl = 3.0
I = Vs / (Rs + Rl)
print(round(I, 4))
Vl = I * Rl
print(round(Vl, 4))
Is = Vs / Rs
print(round(Is, 4))
I2 = Is * Rs / (Rs + Rl)
print(round(I2, 4))
V2 = I2 * Rl
print(round(V2, 4))

traps: Reversing the current-source arrow. The head must point at the node that was the + terminal of the voltage source; flip it and every later current carries the wrong sign.
Transforming an ideal source. With R_s = 0 the equivalent current is infinite; with nothing in parallel the equivalent voltage is infinite. Only practical sources transform.
Leaving the resistor in both places. The series R_s and the parallel R_s are one and the same resistor, now moved; it is no longer in series after the swap.
Swallowing the load into the transformation. The equivalence holds only at the two kept terminals, so the load stays outside.
Comparing internal power instead of terminal quantities. In the example the voltage model's source gives 64 W and the current model's gives 32 W, yet the load takes 21.33 W in both cases.

quiz.q: State the source transformation rule for a voltage source V_s in series with R_s.
quiz.a: It becomes a current source I_s = V_s/R_s in parallel with the same R_s, with the arrow pointing at the node that was the + terminal of V_s.

quiz.q: Which sources cannot be transformed, and why?
quiz.a: Ideal sources. An ideal voltage source has R_s = 0, giving infinite equivalent current; an ideal current source has no parallel resistance, giving infinite equivalent voltage.

quiz.q: Why do the two models deliver the same terminal current for every load resistance?
quiz.a: Both give the same line V = V_s − I·R_s when V_s = I_s·R_s. One V-I relation at the terminals means one behaviour, whatever load is attached.

quiz.q: A 12 V source has 4 Ω in series. Transform it and mark the arrow direction.
quiz.a: I_s = V_s/R_s = 12/4 = 3 A, in parallel with 4 Ω. The arrow points at the node that was the + terminal of the 12 V source.

quiz.q: A 4 A source sits in parallel with 2 Ω. Transform it to the voltage form.
quiz.a: V_s = I_s·R_s = 4 × 2 = 8 V, in series with 2 Ω. The + terminal of the 8 V source sits at the node the arrow pointed to.

quiz.q: Two current sources, 3 A and 2 A, each with its own parallel resistance, feed the same node pair with arrows in the same direction. How do you combine them, and what if one arrow is reversed?
quiz.a: Same direction: the currents add to 5 A and the two resistances combine in parallel. If one arrow is reversed, the currents subtract, giving 3 − 2 = 1 A net, with the arrow of the larger source; the resistances still combine in parallel. Transform back to the voltage form afterwards if the rest of the circuit wants it.

quiz.q: A 10 V source with 5 Ω series feeds a 10 Ω load. Transform it and show that the load power is unchanged but the ideal source's output power is not.
quiz.a: Voltage model: total resistance 5 + 10 = 15 Ω, current = 10/15 = 0.6667 A, load voltage = 6.667 V, load power = 4.444 W. Source output = 10 × 0.6667 = 6.667 W. Transformed: I_s = 10/5 = 2 A in parallel with 5 Ω, and 5 Ω ∥ 10 Ω = 3.333 Ω, so V = 2 × 3.333 = 6.667 V and load current = 0.6667 A, load power 4.444 W. Source output = 2 × 6.667 = 13.33 W. Terminal quantities match; the internal source powers 6.667 W and 13.33 W differ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators assemble their nodal matrix from current sources, so every voltage source in a netlist is converted to a Norton pair internally, which is why a series resistance is expected beside each one. Battery and cell datasheets quote internal resistance exactly so that the terminal-sag model can be fitted and used in source transformation. The same equivalence grows into the Norton and Thevenin pair you meet in Unit 2, and extends there to dependent sources. Search 'Norton equivalent derivation' or 'source transformation solved problems' to practise.
